hero.subtitle: GreenMind analyzes plant bioelectrical signals to detect stress earlier and specifically improve cultivation strategies.
hero.note: GreenMind is under development. We are looking for partners for first field tests.

problem.title2: when the damage is already visible.
problem.description: Today, sensors monitor the environment — temperature, humidity, soil moisture. But not the plant itself. However, plants send out bioelectrical signals that indicate stress — often before external symptoms become visible.

solution.title: Understanding plant signals. Acting more specifically.
solution.description: GreenMind records bioelectrical signals directly on the plant and makes them usable for data-driven cultivation decisions.

earlyStress.title: Early stress detection
earlyStress.description: Bioelectrical signals can indicate drought, pest, and nutrient stress — aiming to identify problems before visible damage occurs.

dataPlanning.title: Data-driven yield planning
dataPlanning.description: Plant signals combined with environmental data enable new approaches for yield planning — data-driven instead of purely experience-based.

resources.title: Targeted resource use
resources.description: When the plant signals what it needs, water and nutrients can be used as needed — lower consumption, better results.

howItWorks.title: From signal to recommendation.
howItWorks.description: Plants react to their environment with measurable electrical signals. GreenMind makes these signals visible and analyzable.

s1.title: Plant signal
s1.description: Plants generate electrical signals in response to changes in their environment — light, water, temperature, nutrients.

s2.title: Sensors
s2.description: Sensors on the plant capture these signals non-invasively and combine them with environmental data like temperature and soil moisture.

s3.title: Analysis
s3.description: The data is automatically processed, filtered, and examined for patterns — which signals indicate which stress?

s4.title: Recommendation
s4.description: Insights are translated into concrete action recommendations — when to water, when to fertilize, when to intervene.

foundation.title: Scientifically grounded. Field-tested.
foundation.description: Developed in collaboration with FHNW and building on peer-reviewed research in plant electrophysiology.
foundation.f1: University of Applied Sciences Northwestern Switzerland

i1.title: Early stress detection
i1.description: Detect plant stress before it becomes visible — through the analysis of bioelectrical signal patterns.

i2.title: Better yield planning
i2.description: Plant signals and environmental data combined allow for more informed forecasts for harvest preparation.

i3.title: Targeted watering and fertilizing
i3.description: Apply water and nutrients exactly when the plant needs them — not according to a rigid schedule.

i4.title: Faster risk detection
i4.description: Identify pest infestations or diseases early and take targeted countermeasures.

i5.title: Lower resource consumption
i5.description: Reduce the ecological footprint through the demand-driven use of water and energy.

i6.title: Data-driven decisions
i6.description: From gut feeling to evidence — make cultivation decisions based on real plant data.

Public.p0003: Understanding plant bioelectrical signals to improve cultivation.
Public.p0005: Agriculture currently monitors temperature, light and soil moisture, but not the condition of the plant itself. GreenMind aims to change this. We are developing a system that records plant bioelectrical signals and makes them useful for better cultivation decisions. A GreenMind GmbH project in collaboration with FHNW.
Public.p0007: Global food demand is rising. Water and farmland are under pressure. Climate variability makes conventional cultivation less predictable. Plants continuously emit electrical signals that can indicate stress, often before visible damage appears. GreenMind investigates whether these signals can inform better cultivation decisions.
Public.p0010: Each component is tested under real cultivation conditions, in greenhouses and outdoors, together with FHNW and agricultural partners. We document our findings in the Science Center and compare them with current scientific literature.
Public.p0013: Are you researching plant bioelectrical signals or operating a cultivation environment that could serve as a research site? We welcome scientific exchange.

Public.p0053: From field data acquisition to dashboard analysis: the areas we are working on.
Public.p0057: Our technology builds on peer-reviewed research in plant electrophysiology. Explore the scientific foundations, from bioelectrical signals to data-driven stress classification.
Public.p0061: Adjust your search or category to find publications.
Public.p0072: How we record and process plant bioelectrical signals and turn them into useful insights for cultivation.
Public.p0074: Plants respond to changes in their environment with measurable electrical signals: light, water availability, temperature, nutrients and pest infestation. Scientific studies show that these signals contain stress-related information that conventional environmental sensors cannot provide.
Public.p0075: GreenMind records these signals directly on the plant, non-invasively and continuously. Combined with conventional environmental data such as temperature and soil moisture, this provides a comprehensive picture of the plant’s condition.
Public.p0078: The system has three layers: ESP32-based sensor units in the field record data and transmit it to Raspberry Pi gateways. The gateways store data locally and forward it to the central server. Local storage ensures that measurements are not lost, even during connection interruptions.
Public.p0079: Communication between field gateways and the server is encrypted using HTTPS. Each gateway authenticates with its own API key.

Public.p0127: Peter spent more than two decades as a Research Scientist at MIT Sloan School of Management and is an honorary professor at the University of Cologne. His current research at Galaxylabs.org focuses on wellbeing, human–animal communication and human–plant communication. With a PhD in computer science from the University of Zurich and postdoctoral experience at MIT, he brings expertise in collaborative intelligence and data-driven research to GreenMind.
Public.p0129: Traver studies data science at FHNW and combines his studies with practical research at GreenMind. After completing vocational training as a physics laboratory technician at armasuisse, he gained experience in data analysis, electronics and sensors. He connects sensor hardware with intelligent data analysis and is responsible for platform development, sensor integration and the data pipeline.
Public.p0131: Distinguishing types of stress through bioelectrical signals: drought, pests and nutrient deficiency. The goal is automatic classification based on collected long-term data.
Public.p0133: Sensors designed for real conditions: high humidity, UV exposure, dust and temperature fluctuations from −5 °C to +50 °C.
Public.p0135: A scalable pipeline for continuous acquisition, processing and long-term storage of measurements, supporting long-term studies and controlled experiments.
Public.p0137: Measurement visualisation with configurable resolution, from raw data to daily averages, synchronised displays and interactive time navigation.
Public.p0139: Structured CSV/ZIP export of sensor data for use in analysis tools, with defined formats to support reproducibility.
Public.p0141: Central management of measurement stations, with availability monitoring, remote configuration and automatic reset when hardware is replaced.
Public.p0143: Sensors on the plant record bioelectrical signals alongside environmental data: temperature, light, humidity and soil moisture. All measurements are synchronised on a shared timeline.
Public.p0145: Raw data is automatically filtered, normalised and prepared as time series for analysis. Patterns and deviations are identified as a basis for interpretation.
Public.p0147: Signal patterns are compared with documented stress events to investigate relationships between plant signals and real field conditions.
Public.p0149: Flexible organic multielectrode arrays map Venus flytrap action potentials at high resolution. The study demonstrates precise, non-invasive recording of plant bioelectrical signals, providing a technical foundation for GreenMind’s sensors.
Public.p0150: Development of conformable organic electrochemical transistor arrays (OECTs) for mapping action potentials over large areas of plant tissue with high spatial and temporal resolution.
Public.p0152: Peter Gloor reports classification of environmental conditions with 85.4% accuracy and human emotions with 73% accuracy using bioelectrical signals from a purple-heart plant. The study illustrates the potential of machine learning for analysing signals of the kind recorded by GreenMind.
Public.p0153: Study of environmental and emotional state classification using bioelectrical signals from Tradescantia pallida, recorded with an AD8232 sensor and analysed with CNN models.
Public.p0155: Peter Gloor reports measurable differences in plant bioelectrical recordings when a person moves nearby. Random Forest classifiers achieve 62.7% accuracy across 2,978 samples from three plant species, providing further evidence of responses to environmental changes in plant bioelectrical recordings.
Public.p0156: Bioelectrical recordings from 2,978 plant samples (basil, lettuce and tomato) are classified using Random Forest and CNN models to detect statistically significant differences between recordings with and without nearby human movement.
Public.p0158: Electrical impedance measurements on plant stems detect water stress with up to 95% correlation with soil moisture. This offers a low-cost way to assess plant needs directly, in line with GreenMind’s sensor approach.
Public.p0159: In-vivo impedance measurements on plant stems show a significant correlation with environmental parameters. The method enables direct, low-cost monitoring of plant condition in real time without visual inspection.
Public.p0160: Electrophysiological signals are used to identify nutrient deficiencies in greenhouse plants. The study is relevant to GreenMind’s aim of assessing both water stress and nutrient deficiencies directly on the plant.
Public.p0161: Use of electrophysiological signals for advanced assessment of nutrient deficiencies in greenhouse environments.
Public.p0162: This foundational work shows plant responses to environmental stress through action and variation potentials, from pests and pesticides to heavy metals. It provides a scientific basis for using plants as living biosensors, as pursued by GreenMind.
Public.p0163: Review of plants as rapid biosensors for detecting light direction, insect attacks, pesticides, uncouplers and heavy-metal exposure through electrical signals.
Public.p0164: Comprehensive review of methods for detecting heavy metals in plants, including non-invasive measurements. Relevant to GreenMind because heavy-metal exposure affects plant biomarkers and electrical signals.
Public.p0165: Systematic review of methods for analysing and detecting heavy-metal concentrations in plants, from ICP-MS and XRF to non-invasive micro-test techniques and omics approaches.
Public.p0166: Hedera helix is equipped with a PhytoNode wearable that records electrophysiological signals outdoors over five months. AutoML classifiers achieve F1 scores of up to 95%, illustrating the potential of plant electrical signals for environmental monitoring under real conditions.
Public.p0167: A biohybrid system uses a plant-wearable PhytoNode device to continuously record the electrophysiological activity of Hedera helix. AutoML approaches outperform manual tuning, with F1 scores up to 95%.
Public.p0168: Machine-learning classifiers (Random Forest and SVC) distinguish tomato ripening stages from electrophysiological signals with over 80% accuracy. The study shows that plant electrical activity of the kind recorded by GreenMind can also reflect developmental processes in fruit.
Public.p0169: Electrical activity in tomato fruit (Solanum lycopersicum var. cerasiforme) is recorded as voltage variations during ripening and analysed using FFT, wavelet transforms, PSD and approximate entropy. Machine-learning methods including Random Forest, SVC and KNN classify three ripening stages (Mature Green, Breaker and Light Red) with accuracy up to 80.76%.
